label: sim-cc-ambiguity-struggling-2
source: simulated demo student (persona: struggling) run through the real platform
content: I will try to answer. 1. First parse: the else belongs to the inner if.   Stmt → if a then (Stmt) else Stmt.  In this tree the inner if is the left child of the first if and the else is attached to that inner if.  Second parse: the else belongs to the outer if.   Stmt → if a then Stmt else Stmt.  Here the left Stmt is the whole inner if, and the else goes to the outer.  2. Most languages choose the first one: else attaches to the nearest unmatched if.  They do this because it keeps code readable and matches human expectation.  3. Unambiguous grammar:  Stmt → Matched | Unmatched.  Matched → if Expr then Matched else Matched | other.  Unmatched → if Expr then Stmt | if Expr then Unmatched else Stmt.  This works because we separate statements that already have else from those that do not, so the parser can decide where else goes without ambiguity.

viva.summary: The student understands the purpose of the nearest‑unmatched‑if rule and can apply it to examples, but their explanation to a beginner is inaccurate and shows some lingering confusion.

rubric.revise_next: Review how to clearly describe the nearest‑unmatched‑if rule in simple terms and practice explaining it without contradictions.

questions.answer: I think the 'nearest unmatched if' means the closest if that doesn’t already have an else, so the parser just pairs the else with that one. That rule sorts the ambiguity because it makes the else go with the closest if that hasn’t got an else yet, but I’m not sure if it covers all cases.
questions.feedback: You correctly identified that the else pairs with the closest if lacking an else, though you were unsure about full coverage.
questions.prompt: In your answer you wrote, "else attaches to the nearest unmatched if." What exactly do you mean by "nearest unmatched if" in this context, and why does that rule resolve the ambiguity?

questions.answer: The first else attaches to the inner if, making that if matched, and the second else attaches to the outer if, so each else goes to the closest if that doesn’t already have one.
questions.feedback: Your prediction of how the two else clauses are assigned matches the standard rule.
questions.prompt: If we have the statement `if x then if y then s1 else s2` and we add another `else s3` after it, how would your "nearest unmatched if" rule assign the two else clauses?

questions.answer: The else will always go to the last if you see, even if it already has an else before it. That means the compiler always pairs it with the outermost unmatched if, not the closest one.
questions.feedback: Your one‑sentence rephrasing is contradictory and misstates the rule.
questions.prompt: If you had to explain the "nearest unmatched if" rule to a beginner programmer in just one sentence, how would you rephrase that part of your answer?

messages.body: How should I start my answer?

Start by naming the outer ‘if’ and then describe the two ways the ‘else’ can be linked – either to the inner ‘if’ or to the outer one – using indentation to show the hierarchy. After that, mention which interpretation most languages adopt and why, and finally give the split grammar with a brief justification. What concrete example will you use to illustrate the first parse tree?
messages.hint: Think about how you would describe each tree step‑by‑step: start with the outermost ‘if’, then show where the ‘else’ is placed.
